title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 814–816 (Night 172, continuing nights-171), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 172 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān asks his vizier what to do about his son's refusal to marry, and the vizier counsels patience: wait one more year, then raise the matter not in private but on a day of public audience, before the emirs, viziers and troops, when the prince will be ashamed to refuse. The king rejoices at the advice and waits, while the youth, nearing twenty, grows ever more beautiful, praised in rhymed prose and in a long poem that swears by each of his charms. The waiting runs its course until a festival day comes, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-second night,
sentences.n: The same pattern as last night: al-thāniya, “the second”, feminine to agree with layla, then wa-al-sabʿūn and baʿda al-miʾa. The alif of المائة is silent: the word is miʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ طَلَبَ وَزِيرَهُ وَاخْتَلَى بِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ قُلْ لِي مَا الَّذِي أَفْعَلُهُ فِي وَلَدِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ قَضِيَّةِ الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika ṭalaba wazīrahu wa-ikhtalā bihi wa-qāla lahu ayyuhā al-wazīru qul lī mā alladhī afʿaluhu fī waladī Qamari al-Zamāni min qaḍiyyati al-zawāji
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the king summoned his-vizier and was-alone with-him and said to-him: O the-vizier, say to-me, what (is) that-which I-do in my-son Qamar al-Zamān from (the) case of the-marriage?
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the king summoned his vizier, took him aside, and said to him, “Vizier, tell me, what am I to do with my son Qamar al-Zamān in this matter of marriage?
sentences.n: Shahrazād again resumes by retelling the last moment of the night before, this time in fewer words: ṭalaba, “to send for, summon”, stands where last night had daʿā bi-. ikhtalā bihi, Form VIII, “to be alone with”: bi- marks the companion; here the print spells it with the final ى. qul lī, “say to me”: qul is the imperative of qāla, and li- marks the one spoken to. For mā alladhī afʿaluhu fī, “what am I to do with”, see the night before.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي اسْتَشَرْتُكَ فِي زَوَاجِهِ فَأَنْتَ الَّذِي أَشَرْتَ عَلَيَّ بِزَوَاجِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ أُسَلْطِنَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-innī istashartuka fī zawājihi fa-anta alladhī asharta ʿalayya bi-zawājihi qabla an usalṭinahu
sentences.l: For indeed-I consulted-you about his-marriage, and you (are) the-one-who advised upon-me with his-marriage before that I-make-him-sultan.
sentences.i: For I consulted you about his marriage, and it was you who advised me to marry him off before I made him sultan.
sentences.n: istashāra, Form X of the root sh-w-r, “to seek advice, consult”; the person consulted is the direct object, -ka. ashāra ʿalā … bi-, Form IV, “to advise someone (ʿalā) to something (bi-)”: ʿalayya is the king himself, bi-zawājihi the advice. usalṭinahu, “I make him sultan”, from the quadriliteral verb salṭana, made from the noun sulṭān; it is a later, non-Classical coinage, here in the subjunctive after an. The shadda of عليّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَذَكَرْتُ لَهُ الزَّوَاجَ مِرَارًا فَخَالَفَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-dhakartu lahu al-zawāja mirāran fa-khālafanī
sentences.l: So I-mentioned to-him the-marriage times-many, and he-opposed-me.
sentences.i: So I spoke to him of marriage again and again, and he went against me.
sentences.n: dhakara li-, “to mention to”: li- marks the one told. mirāran, adverbial accusative, “repeatedly”. khālafa, Form III, “to oppose, go against”, takes its object directly.

sentences.t: فَأَشِرْ عَلَيَّ الْآنَ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ مَا الَّذِي أَفْعَلُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-ashir ʿalayya al-āna ayyuhā al-wazīru mā alladhī afʿaluhu
sentences.l: So advise upon-me now, O the-vizier: what (is) that-which I-do?
sentences.i: So advise me now, Vizier: what am I to do?”
sentences.n: ashir, the imperative of ashāra (Form IV, hollow): the long vowel shortens in the closed syllable, ashir, not ashīr. The hamza and madda of الآن are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ اصْبِرْ عَلَيْهِ سَنَةً أُخْرَى
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru ayyuhā al-maliku iṣbir ʿalayhi sanatan ukhrā
sentences.l: So said to-him the-vizier: O the-king, be-patient upon-him a-year another.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “O king, bear with him one more year.
sentences.n: ṣabara ʿalā, “to be patient with, bear with”: the verb chooses ʿalā. sanatan, accusative of duration, “for a year”.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا أَرَدْتَ أَنْ تُكَلِّمَهُ بَعْدَهَا فِي هَذَا الْأَمْرِ فَلَا تُكَلِّمْهُ سِرًّا وَإِنَّمَا كَلِّمْهُ فِي يَوْمِ حُكُومَةٍ وَيَكُونُ جَمِيعُ الْأُمَرَاءِ وَالْوُزَرَاءِ حَاضِرِينَ وَجَمِيعُ الْعَسَاكِرِ وَاقِفُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā aradta an tukallimahu baʿdahā fī hādhā al-amri fa-lā tukallimhu sirran wa-innamā kallimhu fī yawmi ḥukūmatin wa-yakūnu jamīʿu al-umarāʾi wa-al-wuzarāʾi ḥāḍirīna wa-jamīʿu al-ʿasākiri wāqifūna
sentences.l: And when you-want that you-speak-to-him after-it in this matter, then do-not speak-to-him in-secret; rather speak-to-him in a-day of-government, and (there) will-be all the-emirs and the-viziers present, and all the-troops standing.
sentences.i: Then, when you mean to speak to him of it again, do not do so in private. Speak to him instead on a day of public audience, when all the emirs and viziers are present and the whole army stands in attendance.
sentences.n: lā tukallimhu, prohibitive: lā with the jussive. innamā, “only, rather”. yawm ḥukūma, literally “a day of government”: a day when the king sits in state to judge and give audience. wa-yakūnu … introduces the circumstance: “with all the emirs … being present”. ḥāḍirīna is the accusative predicate of yakūnu. Its partner wāqifūna is nominative, so wa-jamīʿu al-ʿasākiri wāqifūna reads best as a separate nominal clause, “while all the troops are standing”, which Classical grammar allows; only if both were meant to hang on yakūnu would it want wāqifīna. The shadda of سرّا and the kasra and shadda of كلِّمه are printed.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا اجْتَمَعَ هَؤُلَاءِ فَأَرْسِلْ حِينَئِذٍ خَلْفَ وَلَدِكَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فِي تِلْكَ السَّاعَةِ وَأَحْضِرْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā ijtamaʿa hāʾulāʾi fa-arsil ḥīnaʾidhin khalfa waladika Qamari al-Zamāni fī tilka al-sāʿati wa-aḥḍirhu
sentences.l: So when gathered these, then send at-that-time behind your-son Qamar al-Zamān in that hour, and bring-him.
sentences.i: When they are all gathered, send for your son Qamar al-Zamān at that very hour and have him brought in.
sentences.n: arsala khalfa, “to send after”, i.e. to send for someone. aḥḍara, Form IV, “to cause to be present, bring”, imperative aḥḍir. The fatḥa on the wa- of واحضره is printed, as are the hamzas of هؤلاء and حينئذ.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا حَضَرَ فَقُلْ لَهُ عَلَى أَمْرِ الزَّوَاجِ بِحَضْرَةِ الْوُزَرَاءِ وَأَرْبَابِ الدَّوْلَةِ وَأَصْحَابِ الصَّوْلَةِ فَإِنَّهُ لَابُدَّ يَسْتَحِى مِنْهُمْ وَلَا يَقْدِرُ أَنْ يُخَالِفَكَ بِحَضْرَتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā ḥaḍara fa-qul lahu ʿalā amri al-zawāji bi-ḥaḍrati al-wuzarāʾi wa-arbābi al-dawlati wa-aṣḥābi al-ṣawlati fa-innahu lā budda yastaḥī minhum wa-lā yaqdiru an yukhālifaka bi-ḥaḍratihim
sentences.l: So when he-comes, then speak to-him upon the-matter of the-marriage in (the) presence of the-viziers and the-lords of the-state (-awla) and the-holders of the-might (-awla); for indeed-he, no escape, will-be-ashamed before-them, and not he-is-able that he-oppose-you in their-presence.
sentences.i: When he has come, speak to him about marriage before the viziers, the lords of state and the men of power; he will surely be ashamed before them, and will not be able to defy you in their presence.”
sentences.n: Rhyme: al-dawlati / al-ṣawlati. qul lahu ʿalā, “speak to him about”: ʿalā for “about” is a Middle Arabic use (Classical would say ʿan or fī). bi-ḥaḍrati, “in the presence of”: bi- is locative. lā budda, “there is no escape”, here runs straight into the verb yastaḥī without the expected an or min an: “he is bound to be ashamed”. yastaḥī, Form X, “to feel shame, be bashful”, is written with final ى for ي, and is the shortened form of yastaḥyī; istaḥyā min, “to be ashamed before”: min marks the people before whom the shame is felt.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ مِنْ وَزِيرِهِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ فَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَاسْتَصْوَبَ رَآيَهُ فِي ذَلِكَ وَخَلَعَ عَلَيْهِ خِلْعَةً سَنِيَّةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Shahramānu min wazīrihi hādhā al-kalāma fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan wa-istaṣwaba raʾyahu fī dhālika wa-khalaʿa ʿalayhi khilʿatan saniyyatan
sentences.l: So when heard King Shahramān from his-vizier this speech, he-rejoiced a-rejoicing intense, and he-judged-right his-counsel in that, and he-bestowed upon-him a-robe splendid.
sentences.i: When King Shahramān heard these words from his vizier, he was overjoyed; he approved his advice and bestowed a splendid robe of honour on him.
sentences.n: faraḥan shadīdan, a cognate accusative: “rejoiced a great rejoicing”. istaṣwaba, Form X of ṣ-w-b, “to judge correct, approve”. raʾy, “opinion, counsel”: the print sets it رآيه, with madda over the alif, but the word is simply raʾyahu, “his counsel”. khalaʿa ʿalā, “to put a robe of honour on someone”: literally “took off (a robe) upon him”, the verb choosing ʿalā for the person honoured.

sentences.t: وَصَبَرَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ سَنَةً
sentences.tr: wa-ṣabara al-maliku Shahramānu ʿalā waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni sanatan
sentences.l: And was-patient King Shahramān upon his-son Qamar al-Zamān a-year.
sentences.i: So King Shahramān bore with his son Qamar al-Zamān for a year.
sentences.n: The print has ولدة, a misprint for ولده, corrected here. ṣabara ʿalā again, “to bear with”; sanatan, accusative of duration.

sentences.t: وَكُلَّمَا مَرَّتْ عَلَيْهِ يَوْمٌ مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ يَزْدَادُ حُسْنًا وَجَمَالًا وَبَهْجَةً وَكَمَالًا حَتَّى بَلَغَ مِنَ الْعُمْرِ قَرِيبًا مِنْ عِشْرِينَ سَنَةً
sentences.tr: wa-kullamā marrat ʿalayhi yawmun mina al-ayyāmi yazdādu ḥusnan wa-jamālan wa-bahjatan wa-kamālan ḥattā balagha mina al-ʿumri qarīban min ʿishrīna sanatan
sentences.l: And whenever passed over-him a-day of the-days, he-increases (in) loveliness and beauty and radiance and perfection (-ālan), until he-reached of the-age near to twenty years.
sentences.i: And with every day that passed over him he grew in loveliness and beauty, in radiance and perfection, until he was nearly twenty years old.
sentences.n: marrat … yawmun: the verb is feminine though yawm, “day”, is masculine; the text has it so, perhaps by attraction to the plural al-ayyām, which may take a feminine verb. Rhyme: jamālan / kamālan. The accusatives ḥusnan, jamālan … are of specification, “in beauty”. balagha mina al-ʿumri, “reached, in age”: min marks the respect in which; qarīban min, “near to”.

sentences.t: وَأَلْبَسَهُ اللَّهُ حُلَّةَ الْجَمَالِ وَتَوَّجَهُ بِتَاجِ الْكَمَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-albasahu Allāhu ḥullata al-jamāli wa-tawwajahu bi-tāji al-kamāli
sentences.l: And God clothed-him (in) the-robe of-beauty and crowned-him with (the) crown of-perfection.
sentences.i: God had clothed him in the robe of beauty and crowned him with the crown of perfection.
sentences.n: Rhyme: al-jamāli / al-kamāli. albasa, Form IV, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the person and the garment. tawwaja, Form II, “to crown”, with bi- of the instrument: bi-tāji, “with the crown”. The shadda of توّجه is printed.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ طَرْفُهُ أَسْحَرَ مِنْ هَارُوتَ وَغُنْجُ أَلْحَاظِهِ أَضَلَّ مِنَ الطَّاغُوتِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra ṭarfuhu asḥara min Hārūta wa-ghunju alḥāẓihi aḍalla mina al-ṭāghūti
sentences.l: So became his-eye more-bewitching than Hārūt, and (the) coquetry of his-glances more-misleading than the-Ṭāghūt (-ūt).
sentences.i: His eye grew more bewitching than Hārūt, and the coquetry of his glances more beguiling than the idol of error.
sentences.n: Rhyme: Hārūta / al-ṭāghūti. asḥar, elative of sāḥir, “more enchanting”; aḍall, elative of ḍāll, “more astray, more leading astray”; both diptote, with min, “than”. Hārūt is one of the two angels who taught men sorcery in Babylon (Qurʾān 2:102); al-ṭāghūt is the Qurʾānic word for idols or any false object of worship that leads men astray. ghunj, “amorous coquetry”; alḥāẓ, plural of laḥẓ, “glance”.

sentences.t: وَأَشْرَقَتْ خُدُودُهُ بِالِاحْمِرَارِ وَازْدَرَتْ جُفُونُهُ بِالصَّارِمِ الْبَتَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-ashraqat khudūduhu bi-al-iḥmirāri wa-izdarat jufūnuhu bi-al-ṣārimi al-battāri
sentences.l: And shone his-cheeks with the-redness, and scorned his-eyelids the-sword the-cutting (-ār).
sentences.i: His cheeks glowed red, and his eyelids put the keen sword to scorn.
sentences.n: Rhyme: al-iḥmirāri / al-battāri. bi-al-iḥmirāri, “with redness”: bi- of the manner of the shining. The second clause is obscure. Read here as izdarat, Form VIII of z-r-y, “to despise, make light of”, which takes bi- of the thing despised: his eyelids, from which the glance strikes, hold the sharp sword cheap, being keener. Other readings are possible: the print may stand for azrat bi-, Form IV of the same root, “to put to shame”, with a stray dāl, or for a verb of the root z-d-r unknown to the lexicons. ṣārim, “sharp sword”; battār, intensive of bātir, “cutting”.

sentences.t: وَبَيَاضُ غُرَّتِهِ حَكَى الْقَمَرَ الزَّاهِرَ وَسَوَادُ شَعْرِهِ كَأَنَّهُ اللَّيْلُ الْعَاكِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-bayāḍu ghurratihi ḥakā al-qamara al-zāhira wa-sawādu shaʿrihi kaʾannahu al-laylu al-ʿākiru
sentences.l: And (the) whiteness of his-forehead resembled the-moon the-shining (-āhir), and (the) blackness of his-hair, as-if-it (were) the-night the-murky (-ākir).
sentences.i: The whiteness of his brow was like the shining moon, and the blackness of his hair like the murky night.
sentences.n: Rhyme: al-zāhira / al-ʿākiru. ḥakā, “to relate”, also means “to resemble, imitate”, as here. kaʾannahu: the clause begins with sawādu shaʿrihi and is picked up by -hu, “as if it were”. al-ʿākir is unusual: it seems to be an active participle from ʿakira, “to be turbid, murky”, said of water thick with sediment and of night growing dark; the usual words would be al-dājī or al-ʿakir. It may be a coinage for the rhyme. The hamza of كأنه is printed.

sentences.t: وَخَصْرُهُ أَرَقُّ مِنْ خَيْطِ هِمْيَانٍ وَرِدْفُهُ أَثْقَلُ مِنَ الْكُثْبَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-khaṣruhu araqqu min khayṭi himyānin wa-ridfuhu athqalu mina al-kuthbāni
sentences.l: And his-waist (is) finer than (the) thread of-a-money-belt (-ān), and his-buttock heavier than the-sand-hills (-ān).
sentences.i: His waist was finer than the cord of a purse-belt, and his hips heavier than the dunes of sand.
sentences.n: Rhyme: himyānin / al-kuthbāni. araqq, elative of raqīq, “thin, fine”; athqal, of thaqīl, “heavy”: the slender waist above full hips is the stock ideal of beauty, for boys as for girls. himyān, a belt or girdle in which money is carried; kuthbān, plural of kathīb, “sand-hill”. The shadda of ارقّ is printed.

sentences.t: تَهَيَّجَ الْبَلَابِلُ عَلَى أَعْطَافِهِ وَيَشْكِي خَصْرُهُ مِنْ ثِقَلِ أَرْدَافِهِ
sentences.tr: tahayyaja al-balābilu ʿalā aʿṭāfihi wa-yashkī khaṣruhu min thiqali ardāfihi
sentences.l: Were-stirred the-anxieties over his-flanks, and complains his-waist of (the) weight of his-hips (-āfihi).
sentences.i: Hearts were thrown into turmoil by the grace of his sides, and his waist complained of the weight of his hips.
sentences.n: The print has خصرة, a misprint for خصره (khaṣruhu), corrected here. Rhyme: aʿṭāfihi / ardāfihi. tahayyaja, Form V, “to be stirred up”, read here as a perfect; it could also be the imperfect tahayyaju, with one of its two ta- dropped, to match yashkī. al-balābil, “cares, agitations of the heart” (pl. of balbala), punning on balābil, “nightingales”. ʿiṭf, “side, flank”, and its plural aʿṭāf speak of a supple, swaying figure. yashkī for Classical yashkū, “he complains”: the verb treated as if its last root letter were y, a Middle Arabic form. shakā min, “to complain of”: min marks the cause. The shadda of تهيّج is printed.

sentences.t: وَمَحَاسِنُهُ حَيَّرَتِ الْوَرَى كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ بَعْضُ الشُّعَرَاءِ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-maḥāsinuhu ḥayyarati al-warā ka-mā qāla fīhi baʿḍu al-shuʿarāʾi hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And his-charms bewildered the-mankind, as said about-him some (of) the-poets these verses:
sentences.i: His charms bewildered all mankind, as a poet said of him in these lines:
sentences.n: maḥāsin, “good points, charms”, a plural with no singular in use. ḥayyara, Form II, “to perplex, bewilder”; the broken plural takes a feminine verb. ka-mā, “just as”: ka- compares. qāla fīhi, “said of him”: fī marks the subject of the verses.

sentences.t:
قَسَمًا بِوَجْنَتِهِ وَبَاسِمِ ثَغْرِهِ * وَبِاَسْهُمٍ قَدْ رَاشَهَا مِنْ سِحْرِهِ
وَبِلِينِ عِطْفَيْهِ وَمُرْهَفِ لَحْظِهِ * وَبَيَاضِ غُرَّتِهِ وَاَسْوَدِ شَعْرِهِ
وَبِحَاجِبٍ حَجَبَ الْكَرَي عَنْ نَاظِرِي * وَسَطَا عَلَيَّ بِنَهْيِهِ وَبِاَمْرِهِ
وَعَقَارِبٍ قَدْ اُرْسِلَتْ مِنْ صُدْغِهِ * وَسَعَتْ لِقَتْلِ الْعَاشِقِينَ بِهَجْرِهِ
وَبِوَرْدِ خَدَّيْهِ وَاسِ عِذَارِهِ * وَعَقِيقِ مَبْسَمِهِ وَلُؤْلُؤِ ثَغْرِهِ
وَبِطِيبِ نَكْهَتِهِ وَسَلْسَالٍ جَرَى * فِي فِيهِ يُزْرِي بِالرَّحِيقِ وَعَصْرِهِ
وَبِرِدْفِهِ الْمُرْتَجِّ فِي حَرْكَاتِهِ * وَسُكُونِهِ وَبِرِقَّةٍ فِي خَصْرِهِ
وَبِجُودِ رَاحَتِهِ وَصِدْقِ لِسَانِهِ * وَبِطِيبِ عُنْصُرِهِ وَعَالِي قَدْرِهِ
مَا الْمِسْكُ اِلَّا مِنْ فُضَالَةِ خَالِهِ * وَالطِّيبُ يَرْوِي رِيحَهُ عَنْ نَشْرِهِ
وَكَذَلِكَ الشَّمْسُ الْمُنِيرَةُ دُونَهُ * وَارَى الْهِلَالَ قُلَامَةً مِنْ ظَفْرِهِ
sentences.tr:
qasaman bi-wajnatihi wa-bāsimi thaghrihi * wa-bi-ashumin qad rāshahā min siḥrihi
wa-bi-līni ʿiṭfayhi wa-murhafi laḥẓihi * wa-bayāḍi ghurratihi wa-aswadi shaʿrihi
wa-bi-ḥājibin ḥajaba al-karā ʿan nāẓirī * wa-saṭā ʿalayya bi-nahyihi wa-bi-amrihi
wa-ʿaqāribin qad ursilat min ṣudghihi * wa-saʿat li-qatli al-ʿāshiqīna bi-hajrihi
wa-bi-wardi khaddayhi wa-āsi ʿidhārihi * wa-ʿaqīqi mabsamihi wa-luʾluʾi thaghrihi
wa-bi-ṭībi nakhatihi wa-salsālin jarā * fī fīhi yuzrī bi-al-raḥīqi wa-ʿaṣrihi
wa-bi-ridfihi al-murtajji fī ḥarkātihi * wa-sukūnihi wa-bi-riqqatin fī khaṣrihi
wa-bi-jūdi rāḥatihi wa-ṣidqi lisānihi * wa-bi-ṭībi ʿunṣurihi wa-ʿālī qadrihi
mā al-misku illā min fuḍālati khālihi * wa-al-ṭību yarwī rīḥahu ʿan nashrihi
wa-ka-dhālika al-shamsu al-munīratu dūnahu * wa-arā al-hilāla qulāmatan min ẓufrihi
sentences.l:
(I swear) an-oath by his-cheek and (the) smiling of his-mouth, * and by arrows (that) he-has feathered-them from his-magic (-rihi),
and by (the) suppleness of his-two-flanks and (the) keen-edge of his-glance, * and (the) whiteness of his-forehead and (the) black of his-hair (-rihi),
and by a-brow (that) barred the-sleep from my-eye * and lorded over-me with his-forbidding and with his-command (-rihi),
and scorpions (that) have-been-let-loose from his-temple * and have-hastened to-(the)-killing of the-lovers with his-forsaking (-rihi),
and by (the) rose of his-two-cheeks and (the) myrtle of his-cheek-down, * and (the) carnelian of his-smiling-place and (the) pearl of his-teeth (-rihi),
and by (the) sweetness of his-breath, and a-limpid-water (that) runs * in his-mouth, putting-to-shame the-choice-wine and its-pressing (-rihi),
and by his-hindquarters, the-quivering in his-movements * and his-stillness, and by a-slenderness in his-waist (-rihi),
and by (the) bounty of his-palm and (the) truth of his-tongue, * and by (the) goodness of his-stock and (the) high-one of his-rank (-rihi):
not (is) the-musk except from (the) leftover of his-beauty-spot, * and the-perfume relates its-scent from his-fragrance (-rihi);
and likewise the-sun, the-shining-one, (is) beneath-him, * and I-see the-crescent (as) a-paring of his-fingernail (-rihi).
sentences.n: Kāmil metre, fully pointed in the print and copied as printed; the rhyme is -rihi, and the pronoun -hi is lengthened to -hī in scansion. Another version of this poem, also of ten lines but differing in wording throughout and with two of its lines replaced by others, is quoted in Night 17. The whole poem is one oath. qasaman, “(I swear) an oath”, is an accusative standing for its own verb, and bi- is the bi- of swearing, “by”. Each later wa- carries the oath on, whether or not bi- is repeated after it (wa-bāsimi, wa-bayāḍi, wa-ʿaqāribin and the rest are all genitives still hanging on bi-). The answer of the oath, what is sworn to, comes only in the ninth line: mā al-misku illā …, “musk is nothing but …”. As usual in its verse, the print writes hamza as a bare alif with a vowel: bi-ashumin, aswadi, bi-amrihi, ursilat, illā, arā; and it writes ās, “myrtle”, as وَاسِ without the madda. ashum is a plural of sahm, “arrow”; rāsha is to fit an arrow with its feathers, and the arrows are his glances. ḥājib, “eyebrow”, is also “chamberlain”, the officer who keeps the door, so the brow ḥajaba, “barred”, sleep from the poet's eye and rules him with forbidding and command, as a chamberlain would. ḥajaba … is a relative clause on an indefinite noun, with no alladhī, the regular construction; so too qad ursilat and jarā below. The print writes al-karā, “sleep”, with a dotted ي for ى. ʿaqārib, “scorpions”, are the curled locks on his temples (ṣudgh), a stock image; ʿaqārib is a diptote and would not normally take tanwīn, but poetry may give it one for the metre, and the metre here needs ʿaqāribin. The verbs ursilat and saʿat are feminine singular because their subject is a non-human plural. ʿidhār is the first down on the cheek, here a green myrtle beside the rose of the cheek; ʿaqīq, “carnelian”, is the red of the lips, and mabsam, “the place of smiling”, is the mouth. thaghr, “mouth, front teeth”, closes both the first and the fifth line. salsāl is sweet, cool water that slips easily down the throat, here his saliva; fī fīhi is “in his mouth”, fī the preposition and then fī, the genitive of fū/fam, “mouth”. azrā bi- is “to make light of, put to shame”: the verb takes bi- for what it belittles. ʿaṣrihi, “its pressing”, is the pressing of the grapes that makes the wine. ridf, “hindquarters”, is praised in love poetry for heaviness and a quiver; al-murtajj, Form VIII of rajja, “quivering”. The print points ḥarkātihi, with a sukūn, for Classical ḥarakātihi; both readings scan, and the print's is kept. ʿunṣur, “origin, stock”; ʿālī qadrihi, literally “the high of his rank”, an adjective put in construct with the thing it describes. khāl, “mole, beauty spot”, is black, like musk, so all the world's musk is only what is left over from it. yarwī ʿan is the language of ḥadīth transmission: perfume “relates” its scent on the authority of his. dūnahu, “beneath him”, means inferior to him. وَارَى is read wa-arā, “and I see”, with arā taking two objects, “I see the crescent as a paring”; the letters could also be read wārā, “he concealed”, which gives no sense here. The print points the last word ظَفْرِهِ, with a fatḥa; the word for nail is ẓufr, and it is read so.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ سَمِعَ كَلَامَ الْوَزِيرِ سَنَةً أُخْرَى حَتَّى حَصَلَ يَوْمُ مَوْسِمٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika Shahramāna samiʿa kalāma al-wazīri sanatan ukhrā ḥattā ḥaṣala yawmu mawsimin
sentences.l: Then indeed the-king Shahramān heard (the) speech of the-vizier another year, until came-about a-day of festival
sentences.i: Then King Shahramān heeded his vizier's words for another year, until a festival day came round
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, is the narrator's usual way of moving the story on; it puts al-malika in the accusative, with Shahramāna in apposition (a diptote, so -a). samiʿa kalāma, “heard the words of”, here means heeded, went along with the vizier's counsel. sanatan ukhrā, “another year”, is an accusative of duration. ḥaṣala, “came about, arrived”; yawmu mawsimin, “a day of festival”: mawsim is a season of gathering, a festival or fair, and also the season of the pilgrimage. The sentence breaks off here: dawn overtakes Shahrazād before she can tell what happened on that festival day, and the next night takes it up.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahra Zāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And overtook Shahra Zād the-morning (-āḥ), and she-fell-silent from the-speech the-permitted (-āḥ).
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, rhyming al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi. The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning. The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept.
